planting.note: Plant bulbs, or divisions 'in the green', in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; the broad, gray-green leaves fold back at the margins as they emerge, a distinctive trait separating this species from the common snowdrop.

directions: Plant bulbs 3 to 4 inches deep in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade beneath deciduous trees. Pleated snowdrop is distinguished from the common snowdrop by its broader, glaucous leaves, whose margins fold backward like a pleat as they emerge, and by its typically larger flowers, which often carry a green mark on both inner and outer petal segments. Native to woodlands around the Black Sea, it parented many of the best-known garden snowdrop hybrids. Establishment is slow the first year or two, but clumps bulk up steadily once settled and can be divided immediately after flowering.

planting.note: Plant bulbs, or divisions taken 'in the green' just after flowering, in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Magnet is prized for its unusually long, thread-like flower stalks that let each bloom swing freely in the slightest breeze.

directions: Plant bulbs 3 to 4 inches deep in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, ideally under deciduous trees or shrubs. Magnet is one of the most recognizable historic snowdrop cultivars, dating from the 1880s, named for the unusually long, wire-thin pedicels that suspend each large, rounded flower so it sways at the slightest air movement. It bulks up into generous clumps at a moderate pace and is a reliable, widely available choice for gardeners wanting a distinctive snowdrop beyond the common single form. Divide congested clumps immediately after flowering while the foliage is still green for best transplant success.

common_name: Blue Giant Glory-of-the-Snow (Large True-Blue Chionodoxa Selection)

planting.note: Plant bulbs 3 inches deep and 3 inches apart in well-drained soil in fall, 4-8 weeks before first frost; Blue Giant produces noticeably larger, richer-blue flower clusters than the straight species and is often sold paired with 'Pink Giant'.

directions: Plant bulbs 3 inches deep in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade in fall for very early spring bloom. Blue Giant is a robust selection of glory-of-the-snow bred for larger flower clusters and a deeper, more saturated gentian-blue color than the wild species, while keeping the same small white central eye and grass-like foliage. It blooms alongside the pink-flowered 'Pink Giant' cultivar already common in trade, making an easy two-tone underplanting beneath deciduous shrubs or a lawn edge. Like the species, it self-seeds and naturalizes readily once established, forming expanding colonies with minimal care.

planting.note: Plant bulbs 4-6 inches deep in fall in moist, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Alba is a pure white-flowered selection that holds its color best in cooler climates.

directions: Plant bulbs 4-6 inches deep in organically rich, moisture-retentive soil in full sun to partial shade; like the species, Alba tolerates seasonally wet spring conditions better than most bulbs. It sends up the same tall, stately flower spikes as the species in late spring, but the individual star-shaped blooms are clean ivory-white rather than violet-blue, making a striking companion planted alongside blue-flowered camassia cultivars or ornamental grasses. Allow the foliage to yellow and die back naturally after flowering to recharge the bulb, and leave clumps undisturbed for several years to build into substantial naturalized drifts.

planting.note: Plant large bulbs on their side 6-8 inches deep in fall in fertile, sharply drained soil in full sun; planting on the side keeps water from pooling in the hollow crown and rotting the bulb.

directions: Plant large bulbs on their side 6-8 inches deep in fertile, sharply drained soil in full sun, since the hollow-crowned bulb rots easily if water collects in it. Lutea is the classic yellow-flowered counterpart to the orange-red 'Rubra Maxima', producing the same dramatic tall stalk topped by a ring of large, nodding, bell-shaped flowers, here in clear golden-yellow, beneath a tuft of leafy bracts. The whole plant carries a distinctive musky odor, especially near the bulb, that most gardeners find unpleasant but that reliably repels deer, voles, and squirrels. Leave foliage to die back undisturbed after bloom, and avoid moving or dividing established clumps, since crown imperial dislikes transplanting.

planting.note: Plant bulbs 4-5 inches deep in fall in sharply drained soil in full sun to light shade; this species is markedly easier and more reliable in garden conditions than most other fritillaries.

directions: Plant bulbs 4-5 inches deep in gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun to light shade in fall, choosing a spot that stays relatively dry over summer once the plant goes dormant. Native to rocky hillsides of Turkey, Syria, and Lebanon, pointed fritillary sends up wiry stems bearing one or two nodding, bell-shaped flowers that are apple-green outside and washed with maroon-brown toward the sharply pointed, slightly recurved tepal tips that give the species its name. It is considerably easier to establish than the checkered or crown fritillaries, tolerating a wider range of garden soils, and slowly naturalizes by offsets and self-seeding in a rock garden or sunny border. Leave foliage to ripen and yellow fully before cutting back.

common_name: Guinea Gold Winter Aconite (Large-Flowered Sterile Hybrid Aconite)

planting.note: Plant tubers as fresh as possible in late summer to early fall, 2-3 inches deep, in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade; soak dry tubers 24 hours before planting, since this sterile hybrid must be grown from tubers rather than seed.

directions: Plant tubers 2-3 inches deep as early in fall as they can be obtained, in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade beneath deciduous trees. Guinea Gold is a vigorous hybrid between Eranthis hyemalis and E. cilicica, bearing noticeably larger, deeper golden-yellow flowers and bronze-tinted young foliage compared with the straight winter aconite species, and it tends to bloom a little later, extending the late-winter display. Because the cross is sterile and sets no viable seed, it increases only slowly by division of the tuber clumps, so established colonies should be left largely undisturbed once planted. It pairs beautifully with snowdrops, opening at the same time for one of the earliest color combinations of the gardening year.

common_name: Kondo Trout Lily (Pale Yellow Multi-Flowered Hybrid Fawn Lily)

planting.note: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil under deciduous shade; Kondo typically carries two or more flowers per stem, more than most wild trout lily species.

directions: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep and 4-6 inches apart in fall in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained woodland soil, then leave undisturbed to naturalize. Kondo is a Dutch-raised hybrid trout lily bearing mottled green leaves and nodding, pale creamy-yellow, reflexed flowers with a soft greenish-bronze base, typically two to three blooms per sturdy stem, giving a fuller floral display than most single-flowered wild species. It has earned an RHS Award of Garden Merit for its combination of vigor, hardiness, and reliable multiplication in the garden. Foliage dies back by early summer, so pair it with later-emerging shade perennials such as ferns or hostas to fill the gap it leaves behind.

common_name: Roseum White Trillium (Natural Pink-Flowered Color Form)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic woodland soil in partial to full shade, setting 2-3 inches deep with the growing tip up; because color does not come reliably true from seed, propagate this form only by division to preserve the pink flower color.

directions: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic woodland soil in partial to full shade, setting the rhizome 2-3 inches deep with the growing tip pointed upward. Roseum is a naturally occurring color form of white trillium in which the three-petaled flowers open a soft rose-pink from the start, rather than opening white and aging to pink late in the bloom period as ordinary grandiflorum flowers do. It shares the same broad whorl of dark green leaves and slow, steady clump-forming habit as the species, and is prized by woodland gardeners for adding a true pink note to shaded spring plantings. Never collect trilliums from the wild; source only nursery-propagated divisions, since named color forms must be divided rather than grown from seed to keep the coloring consistent.

common_name: Rolf Fiedler Spring Starflower (Deep Gentian-Blue Compact Selection)

planting.note: Plant bulbs 2-3 inches deep in fall in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; Rolf Fiedler is the deepest, truest blue of the commonly grown ipheion cultivars and stays more compact than 'Wisley Blue'.

directions: Plant bulbs 2-3 inches deep in fall in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; spring starflower tolerates dry summer conditions well once established. Rolf Fiedler is a compact, low-growing selection prized for intensely saturated, true gentian-blue, star-shaped flowers, a noticeably deeper and purer blue than the species or most other named ipheion cultivars, held just above narrow, onion-scented, grass-like foliage. It holds RHS Award of Garden Merit recognition and multiplies more slowly than 'Wisley Blue', making it well suited to rock gardens, troughs, and border edges where a smaller, tidier clump is wanted. Allow foliage to die back naturally after bloom before removing it.

planting.note: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep in fall in well-drained, average soil in full sun; this sterile heirloom mutation must be propagated by bulb offsets rather than seed.

directions: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep in any well-drained, average soil in full sun in fall. Feather hyacinth is a curious heirloom sport of the tassel grape hyacinth in which every flower on the spike has mutated into a fine, curling, sterile thread, producing a fluffy, feathery plume of violet-blue filaments in place of the normal bell-shaped flowers, an oddity grown as a garden novelty for centuries. Because it produces no fertile flowers or seed, it can only increase by offsets from the bulb, so established clumps multiply slowly and should be left undisturbed between divisions. It makes an unusual textural accent toward the back of a sunny border or rock garden alongside more conventional spring bulbs.

planting.note: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep in late summer, well before the leafless, checkered flowers push up through the soil in early autumn.

directions: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep and roughly 4-6 inches apart in fertile, well-drained soil during late-summer dormancy, in a spot with sun to light shade. Each corm produces smaller, more refined blooms than the large hybrid colchicums, with a distinctive checkerboard, or tessellated, pattern of light and dark purple-pink across each petal, opening directly from bare ground in early autumn ahead of the strap-shaped leaves that follow the next spring. It naturalizes well in rock gardens, raised beds, or the front of a border where its dainty scale and patterned petals can be appreciated up close. All parts of the plant are toxic if ingested, so keep it away from areas grazed by pets or livestock.
